official_title: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of Alabama of 2022, to provide for the election of a Lieutenant Governor if the Office of Lieutenant Governor becomes vacant during the first two years of a term, to authorize the Legislature to set the salary of the Lieutenant Governor and officers of the Legislature, and to require any expenditure of legislative funds for travel to be approved by a legislative officer. Proposed by Act 2026-341.
plain_summary: Three changes in one. If the lieutenant governor's seat empties early in a term, voters would fill it at the next statewide general election instead of leaving it empty. Lawmakers could set that office's pay and their officers' pay. Lawmakers' travel spending would need an officer's approval.
yes_means: An early lieutenant governor vacancy is filled by election, the Legislature sets that office's pay, and legislative travel spending needs an officer's approval.
no_means: A lieutenant governor vacancy stays open until the next regular election, the Constitution keeps setting the pay, and travel approval rules don't change.
current_law: The Fair Ballot Commission: 'Current law generally provides that if the office of Lieutenant Governor becomes vacant during a term of office, the vacancy remains until the next regular election for that office. The Alabama Constitution also sets the pay of the Lieutenant Governor and certain legislative officers.' In practice, a vacancy before 2028 would leave the seat empty until 2030; under the amendment the state could fill it in 2028.
fiscal_impact: Official statement: 'There are no costs or taxes associated with Amendment 1.'
pass_threshold: simple majority of votes cast on the amendment
confusing_wording_note: The title bundles three unrelated changes, so you can't vote for one and against another. The headline change is the first one: whether an empty lieutenant governor's seat gets filled by voters or can sit empty for years.

supporters_case.text: Sponsor Sen. Sam Givhan said the state needed a way to fill an early vacancy rather than leave the seat empty, and described the measure as a stopgap he may revisit. It passed the Legislature without a dissenting vote.

opponents_case.text: We found no organized campaign or official argument on this side.

official_title: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of Alabama of 2022, to provide a process for the creation of a consolidated county school system by merging two or more contiguous county boards of education; to require the State Board of Education to conduct an impact study on the potential effects of the consolidation; to require publication of the impact study; to provide a procedure for protesting a proposed consolidation of two or more county school systems; and to require the State Board of Education to adopt rules. Proposed by Act 2026-378.
plain_summary: Creates a way for two or more neighboring county school boards to merge into one system. The state must first study and publish the effects. If 25% of voters in any affected county protest in writing, the merger goes to a vote and needs a majority in each county and overall.
yes_means: Neighboring county school boards get a process to merge, with a required state impact study and a voter-protest route that can force an election.
no_means: No such process exists; county school boards stay separate as they are now.
current_law: The Fair Ballot Commission: 'Currently, each county has a board of education that operates independently. A process allowing the merger of two or more county boards of education does not currently exist in the Alabama Constitution.'
fiscal_impact: Official statement: 'There are no costs or taxes associated with Amendment 2.'
pass_threshold: simple majority of votes cast on the amendment
confusing_wording_note: A yes vote doesn't merge any school district. It only creates a process county boards could use later. Whether any districts merge would be decided by the boards, the State Board of Education, and, if voters protest, an election.

supporters_case.text: Sponsored by Rep. Terri Collins, it passed the House 96-2 and the Senate unanimously. Lawmakers paired the merger process with a required state impact study and a voter-protest route that can force an election.

opponents_case.text: We found no organized campaign or official argument on this side.

official_title: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of Alabama of 2022, to require local boards of education to adopt policies requiring each public K-12 school to recite The Pledge of Allegiance to the United States flag at the beginning of each school day; and to require local boards of education to adopt a policy authorizing student-initiated and student-led prayer. Proposed by Act 2026-379.
plain_summary: Puts two school rules into the state constitution. Every local school board would have to require the Pledge of Allegiance at the start of each school day and adopt a policy allowing student-led prayer. Students can opt out of either.
yes_means: School boards must adopt a daily Pledge policy and a student-led prayer policy, both with opt-outs, and the requirement goes in the state constitution.
no_means: The state constitution isn't changed, so neither policy is required by it (a 1976 state law already requires the daily Pledge).
current_law: The Fair Ballot Commission: 'Currently, the Alabama Constitution does not require local boards of education to adopt policies requiring each public K-12 school to conduct the Pledge of Allegiance each school day or to adopt policies allowing student-initiated and student-led prayer.' Separately, Alabama statute has required the daily Pledge in K-12 schools since 1976, and the U.S. Supreme Court (West Virginia v. Barnette, 1943) bars compelling students to recite it.
fiscal_impact: Official statement: 'There are no costs or taxes associated with Amendment 3.'
pass_threshold: simple majority of votes cast on the amendment
confusing_wording_note: Two different ideas share one yes/no. The Pledge half mostly repeats existing state law; the sponsor says the point is to protect it from lawsuits. The prayer half is new: it requires boards to have a student-led prayer policy. The amendment doesn't say who oversees the prayer or where it happens, and an Auburn political scientist said the wording 'could run up against some U.S. Supreme Court decisions.'

supporters_case.text: Sponsor Rep. Reed Ingram says a constitutional amendment would 'eliminate the litigation in the future,' that the Pledge is already law but 'a lot of schools are not doing it,' and that for students without faith at home, 'This gives them that opportunity.' He adds the prayer 'is not going to be led by any certain religion' and 'is not going to be mandatory for that child to sit and listen to it.'

opponents_case.text: League of Women Voters of Alabama president Kim Bailey opposes it, saying it is 'impinging on people's rights' and not allowing people 'to make a choice.' Auburn professor Steven P. Brown raised constitutional concerns about the wording and the lack of school oversight of student-led prayer.

official_title: Proposing an amendment to the Constitution of Alabama of 2022, to require local boards of education to adopt policies requiring each public K-12 school to broadcast or sanction the performance of the first stanza of The Star-Spangled Banner at least once per week during school hours. Proposed by Act 2026-424.
plain_summary: Every local school board would have to require each public K-12 school to play the first verse of the national anthem at least once a week during school hours. Instead of a recording, a board can allow a school-approved band, choir, group or singer to perform it, using the Library of Congress version.
yes_means: Schools must play or allow a performance of the first verse of The Star-Spangled Banner at least once a week, and the rule goes in the state constitution.
no_means: The state constitution isn't changed, and no weekly anthem rule is added.
current_law: The Fair Ballot Commission: 'Currently, the Alabama Constitution does not require local boards of education to adopt policies requiring each public K-12 school to broadcast or allow the performance of the first stanza of The Star-Spangled Banner during school hours.'
fiscal_impact: Official statement: 'There are no costs or taxes associated with Amendment 4.'
pass_threshold: simple majority of votes cast on the amendment
confusing_wording_note: 'Broadcast or sanction the performance' means play a recording or let students perform it. The rule is about the school playing the anthem; it doesn't require any student to sing or stand.

supporters_case.text: Rep. Reed Ingram, speaking for the measure, called it a reminder of citizenship: 'It's important for us not to forget that.' Sponsor Sen. Gerald Allen did not respond to the Reflector's requests for comment.

opponents_case.text: No organized opposition was found. Auburn professor Steven P. Brown said he was less concerned about this one than Amendment 3 because it is 'passive, you are not requiring anybody to do anything.' 27 House members and 5 senators voted no.
